data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's own terms as a methodological rule to maximize informational content and risk exposure, not as an inductive inference of future probability.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If Popper explicitly states that choosing a corroborated theory implies a belief in its future reliability or probability.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the distinction between 'acting on' a theory and 'believing' it to be true collapses in Popper's practical advice.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the concept of verisimilitude is shown to rely on inductive assumptions about the structure of the world.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Popper distinguishes between the logical status of a theory (which remains unproven) and the methodological decision of which theory to test or act upon. Choosing the best-corroborated theory is choosing the one that has survived the severest tests and thus possesses the highest empirical content. This choice is a 'rational guess' aimed at truth (verisimilitude) without claiming that past success guarantees future performance, thereby avoiding the smuggled induction criticized by opponents.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
